INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE∗
Amicus curiae the Brady Center to Prevent Gun Violence (“Brady”) is the nation’s longest-standing
nonpartisan, nonprofit organization dedicated to
reducing gun violence through education, research,
legal advocacy, and political action. Brady works to
free America from gun violence by passing and
defending gun violence prevention laws, reforming the
gun industry, and educating the public about
responsible gun ownership.
Brady has a substantial interest in ensuring that the
Constitution is construed to allow democratically
elected officials to address the nation’s gun violence
epidemic and to safeguard the interest of every
American in being safe in their homes and
communities. Brady has filed numerous briefs as an
amicus curiae in cases involving firearms regulations,
including in this Court. E.g. , Wolford v. Lopez, 609
U.S. 185 (2026);  Bondi v.  VanDerStok, 604 U.S. 458
(2025); United States v. Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680 (2024);
N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1
(2022); District of Columbia v. Heller , 554 U.S. 570
(2008).
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF
ARGUMENT
The Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms
is “[d]erived from English practice” and “secures for
Americans a means of self-defense.” Rahimi, 602 U.S.
at 690. “Like most rights, though, the right secured by
the Second Amendment is not unlimited.” Id. (cleaned

∗  No counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in

funded the brief’s preparation or submission.

2

up). “From Blackstone through the 19th-century cases,
commentators and courts routinely explained that the
right was not a right to k eep and carry any weapon
whatsoever in any manner whatsoever and for
whatever purpose.” Heller, 554 U.S. at 626.
This Court has “not read the Second Amendment to
protect the right of citizens to carry arms for any sort
of confrontation.” Id. at 595 (emphasis in original). It
has, instead, made clear that the right to bear arms for
lawful self-defense is the “ central component” of the
Second Amendment right. Id. at 599 (emphasis in
original); see also McDonald v. City of Chicago , 561
U.S. 742, 767 (2010); Bruen, 597 U.S. at 29. It follows
that the prototypical confrontation for which a citizen
has the right to carry arms is a confrontation in a home
or public place that would justify a person using a
weapon in lawful self-defense.
For that reason—and because Petitioners claim that
millions of Americans possess AR-15s for selfdefense—this brief discusses the scope of the right to
lawful self-defense at the ti me of the adoption of the
Second and Fourteenth Amendments and its
implications for whether the challenged bans on AR-
15s infringe that right.
At common law in England, at the founding of this
country, and through the nineteenth century, selfdefense law did not provide a right to defend one’s self,
family, or property with any amount of force, or in any
manner that one desires. It was a right to use the force
reasonably necessary to defend against an imminent
attack on one’s own person or property, or that of one’s
family. The force used could not be disproportionate to
the threat, lest the defender become the aggressor.
These limitations on the right of lawful self-defense—
necessity, imminence, and proportionality—reflect the
law’s longstanding judgment that human life and

3

liberty of all members of society are valuable and
deserve legal protection. See infra § I.
These limitations make the resolution of the
question presented clear:  the bans on AR-15s and
similar assault rifles do not infringe the Second
Amendment. See infra § II.
AR-15s and similar assault rifles have military
features designed for the U.S. military to use in
offensive combat in the Vietnam War, not for civilian
use in lawful self-defense. They can fire dozens of
rounds in rapid-fire succession with a force so
devastating that they can pierce walls and bulletproof
vests, and kill or maim dozens of people in a matter of
seconds. That lethality makes them attractive to those
seeking to rain down terror or mass destruction, and
far exceeds the force necessa ry or appropriate for the
constitutionally protected purpose of lawful selfdefense in a home or in public spaces. Given their
devastating and frequent us e in mass shootings of
innocent civilians, possession of the banned weapons
can also spread fear and terror amongst the public that
is incompatible with the right to carry arms for lawful
self-defense.
This Court has made clear that the right to keep and
bear arms is not a license to possess a weapon “to
destroy [one’s] neighbor,” nor for “unlawful or
unjustifiable purpose[s],” such as breaching the public
peace. Heller, 554 U.S. at 612 (citation omitted). Since
the founding, it has been understood that legislatures
have the authority to ban the carrying of “dangerous
or unusual weapons.” 4 Blackstone, Commentaries on
the Laws of England 148 (4th ed. 1770); see Heller, 554

4

U.S. at 627. 1  And neither Heller nor its progeny has
given any reason to doubt that “weapons that are most
useful in military service,” such as “M-16 rifles and the
like,” can be banned. 554 U.S. at 627.
The ban on AR-15s and similar assault rifles falls
comfortably within that tradition. It is a permissible
regulation to protect the public from an unusually
dangerous weapon while imposing little, if any, burden
on the ability to use an appropriate firearm for lawful
self-defense.
ARGUMENT
I. Historically, The Right To Self-Defense Was
A Limited Right To Use Force That Is
Reasonably Necessary To Avoid Imminent
Death Or Serious Bodily Injury, And Could
Not Be Disproportionate To The Threat
Presented.
A. Self-defense in the common law of
England.
Because this Court has interpreted the Second
Amendment as codifying a right to bear arms for selfdefense derived from English practice, it is important
to recognize how the Framers understood the English
right.
In English common law, the right to self-defense was
limited to using the amount of force reasonably
necessary to protect one’s own life or property, or that
of one’s family, from immine nt attack. The force used

1 As Respondent Connecticut explains, and Petitioners concede,
this phrase is also formulated as “dangerous and unusual” in
English law, and regardless of phrasing differences, the words are
read together to form a “single, complex idea.”  Br. for the
Connecticut Respondents at 16.

5

could not be disproportionate to the threat, and in
many instances, there was a duty to retreat before
using any force at all.
William Blackstone—the “preeminent authority on
English law for the founding,”  Heller , 554 U.S. at
593—summarized the principles of the English
doctrine in his well-known Commentaries on the Laws
of England.
If a person was “forcibly attacked in his person or
property,” it was “lawful for him to repel force by
force.” 3 William Blackstone, Commentaries on the
Laws of England 3 (4th ed. 1770).  A person could also
use force to repel an attack upon members of one’s
household—a spouse, parent, child, master, or
servant. Id.
Because self-defense was a “right of preventive
defense,” the use of force was lawful only when an
attack was imminent. 4 Blackstone, Commentaries, at
184. A person could use force in self-defense when
attacked “in sudden and violent cases; when certain
and immediate suffering would be the consequence of
waiting for the assistance of the law.” Id.  But a person
could not use force to redres s past injuries or avoid
future injuries that were not imminent. “[I]nstead of
attacking one another for injuries past or impending,
men need only have recourse to the proper tribunals of
justice.” Id.
For an act of self-defense to be lawful, the force used
had to be necessary and pr oportional to the threat.
Deadly force was permitted only when the aggressor
used deadly force: “Where a crime, in itself capital, is
endeavored to be committed by force, it is lawful to
repel that force by the death of the party attempting.”
Id. at 181 (emphasis added). When the aggressor used
lesser force or posed a lesser threat, care had to “be

6

taken, that the resistance does not exceed the bounds
of mere defense and prevention; for then the defender
would himself become an aggressor.” 3 Blackstone,
Commentaries, at 4.
To ensure that the defend er used only the force
necessary to avoid his own death or serious bodily
harm, the law generally imposed a duty to retreat
before using deadly force. According to Blackstone,
“the person, who kills another in his own defense,
should have retreated as far as he conveniently or
safely can, to avoid the viol ence of the assault, before
he turns upon his assailant.” 4 Blackstone,
Commentaries, at 184–85; see also  id.  at 184
(“Wherefore, to excuse homi cide by the plea of selfdefense, it must appear th at the slayer had no other
possible means of escaping from his assailant.”)
Finally, self-defense generally was not an available
defense if the person was the aggressor or a willing
participant in the fight. In that situation, the person
would have to exit the fight and “decline any further
struggle.” Id. at 184. Only if he did so, and “afterwards,
being closely pressed by his antagonist, kills him to
avoid his own destruction,” then the homicide was
“excusable by self-defense.” Id.
B. Self-defense in the Colonies and States in
the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
The principles of self-defense from the English
common law described by Blackstone were well known
and followed in the Colonies and in the States after the
founding.
1. In Colonial America, the provision of the English
Bill of Rights giving Protestants the right to “have
Arms for their Defence suitable to the Conditions, and
as allowed by Law” was viewed as “one of the
fundamental rights of Englishmen.” Heller, 554 U.S.

7

at 593–94 (citation omitted). It was well understood,
however, that this right did not include a right to use
arms offensively to threaten or harm others or breach
the peace. In defending in court the soldiers charged
in the Boston Massacre, John Adams emphasized that
Bostonians had the right to bear arms “for their
defence, not for offence.” Adams’ Argument for the
Defense: 3–4 December 1770,
https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Adams/05-
03-02-0001-0004-0016. “[T]hat distinction,” he said, “is
material and must be attended to.” Id.
2. Following Independence, state courts continued to
look to Blackstone and English common law to define
the right to self-defense in this country. An often-cited
early example is the 1806 trial of Thomas Selfridge.
Selfridge was a prominent Federalist lawyer
charged with manslaughter after he shot and killed
the son of a political rival. See  Jack Tager, Politics,
Honor, and Self-Defense in Post-Revolutionary Boston:
The 1806 Manslaughter Trial of Thomas Selfridge, 37
Hist. J. Mass. 85, 85–88 (2009). Selfridge claimed he
fired in self-defense after the victim struck him with a
heavy cane. Id. at 88.
Justice Isaac Parker drafted jury instructions based
on the principles of self-defense in Blackstone and
English common law. Thomas Lloyd & George Caines,
Trial of Thomas O. Selfridge, Counseller at Law,
Before the Hon. Isaac Parker, Esquire, for Killing
Charles Austin, on the Public Exchange, in Boston 159
(2d ed. 1806),
https://collections.nlm.nih.gov/catalog/nlm:nlmuid-
2571038R-bk. The instructions were published in a
book about the trial and were widely cited thereafter
as authority for the plea of self-defense. See  Tager,
supra, at 86; see also, e.g., State v. Walker, 8 W.L.J.
145 (Ohio C.P. Hamilton Cnty. 1850); People v. Doe, 1

8

Mich. 451, 456–57 (1850); State v. Chandler, 5
La. Ann. 489, 490 (1850).
Justice Parker’s instructions on self-defense had
three components:
First. A man, who, in the lawful pursuit of his
business, is attacked by another under
circumstances which denote an intention to
take away his life, or to do him some
enormous bodily harm; may lawfully kill the
assailant, provided he use all the means in
his power, otherwise, to  save his own life or
prevent the intended harm—such as
retreating as far as he can, or disabling his
adversary without killing him, if it be in his
power.
Secondly. When the attack upon him is so
sudden, fierce and violent, that a retreat
would not diminish, but increase his danger,
he may instantly kill his adversary without
retreating at all.
Thirdly. When from the nature of the attack,
there is reasonable ground to believe that
there is a design to destroy his life, or commit
any felony upon his person, the killing the
assailant will be excusable homicide,
although it should afterwards appear that no
felony was intended.
Lloyd & Caines, supra, at 160.
3. The instructions in Selfridge addressed the
situation where a defendant was resisting an attack
initiated by another person. As in English common
law, if the defendant was the aggressor, he lost the
right to defend himself with deadly force unless he had
first quit the combat and retreated.

9

Take, for example, State v. Hill, 20 N.C. (4 Dev. &
Bat.) 491 (1839). Hill initia ted the confrontation by
striking the deceased, who responded by pulling a
knife and cutting Hill. Hill then fatally stabbed him.
Id. at 492. Citing English authorities, the court said it
is “settled law, that if a man assault another with
malice prepense, even though he should be driven to
the wall, and kill him there to save his own life, he is
yet guilty of murder in respect of his first intent.”  Id.
at 494. The killing was excusable self-defense only if
Hill “had quitted the combat before a mortal blow was
given, if the fierceness of his adversary-permitted, and
retreated as far as he might with safety, and had then
killed his adversary of necessity, to save his own life.”
Id. at 494–95.
4. Decisions in other States imposed similar
requirements, limiting lawful self-defense to
situations in which use of force was defensive,
necessary to avoid imminent injury or death, and not
disproportionate to or in excess of the force necessary
to avoid imminent harm. The Addendum lists
pertinent decisions from each State. A few are
illustrative.
In State v. Wells , the New Jersey Supreme Court
held that “no man is justified or excusable in taking
away the life of another, unless the necessity for so
doing is apparent as the only means of avoiding his
own destruction or some very great injury.” 1 N.J.L.
424, 430 (N.J. Sup. Ct. 1790).  The defense was not
established where the victim was “without any kind of
weapon that might have rendered it necessary for the
prisoner to avail himself of the instrument which
occasioned the death.” Id. ; see also, e.g. , Shorter v.
People, 2 N.Y. 193, 203 (1849) (one struck “with the
naked hand,” with no reason to fear great bodily harm,
“must not return the blow with a dangerous weapon”).

10

In State v. Tackett , the North Carolina Supreme
Court held that “in order to reduce a homicide to
excusable self-defence, it is incumbent upon the
accused to prove that he killed his adversary through
mere necessity in order to avoid immediate death;” a
“slight blow, if it did not threaten[] death or great
bodily injury would not excuse” the use of deadly force.
8 N.C. (1 Hawks) 210, 218–19 (1820).
And in Dyson v. State, Mississippi’s highest court
held that to justify killing in self-defense “there must
be some overt act indicating a present intention to kill
the party or to do him some great personal injury,” and
“the danger of such design being accomplished must be
imminent, that is to say, immediate, pressing, and
unavoidable at the time of [the] killing.” 26 Miss. 362,
388 (1853); see also, e.g., Rippy v. State, 39 Tenn. (2
Head) 217, 220 (1858) (“absolutely necessary to kill at
that moment”).
5. After the Civil War, one difference did emerge
concerning the “ancient doctrine as to the duty of a
person assailed to retreat as far as he can before he is
justified in repelling force by force.” Beard v. United
States, 158 U.S. 550, 561 (1895) (quoting Runyan v.
State, 57 Ind. 80, 83 (1877)). By the end of the
nineteenth century, this Court concluded that the
“weight of modern authority” in this country
establishes “the doctrine that when a person being,
without fault, and in a place where he has a right to
be, is violently assaulted, he may, without retreating,
repel force by force, and if, in the reasonable exercise
of his right of self-defense, his assailant is killed, he is
justifiable.” Id. at 562 (quoting Runyan, 57 Ind. at 84).2

2 The loosening of the duty to retreat would be  irrelevant if the
scope of the right to lawful self-defense were viewed only in terms

11

Not every State followed Beard. To this day, there
are States that retain some duty to retreat.3
Yet even where the duty to  retreat was abandoned,
the other restrictions on the use of force in self-defense
were retained. As Beard explained, to constitute
lawful self-defense, a defendant’s use of force must be
“necessary to save his own life,  or to protect himself
from great bodily injury.” 158 U.S. at 564. Other courts
similarly recognized that “all authorities agree” that
life may be taken in self-defense only “on the ground of
necessity.” Erwin v. State, 29 Ohio St. 186, 199 (1876);
see also, e.g., Runyan, 57 Ind. at 85 (defendant must
have reasonably believed his actions were “necessary

of the common understanding when the Second Amendment was
adopted in 1791. Cf. Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 693, n.1 (noting, but not
resolving,  the “‘ongoing scholarly debate on whether courts
should primarily rely on the prevailing understanding of an
individual right when the Fourteenth Amendment was ratified in
1868’”) (quoting Bruen, 597 U.S. at 37).
3 See, e.g., Conn. Gen. Stat. Ann. § 53a-19 (West 2022) (duty to
retreat except in own dwelling place or place of work, or is a peace
officer acting within the scope of their duties); Del. Code Ann. tit.
11, § 464 (similar); Haw. Rev. Stat. § 703-304 (similar);  Me. Rev.
Stat. Ann. tit. 17-A, § 108 (duty to retreat except in own dwelling);
Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 278, § 8A (duty to retreat except in own
dwelling); Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-1409 (duty to retreat except in
home or at work or when cannot be  done safely); N.J. Stat. Ann.
§ 2C:3-4 (West 2026) (duty to retreat except in home); N.Y. Penal
Law § 35.15 (duty to retreat except in dwelling or when assisting
law enforcement officer); R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-8-8 (duty to retreat
except by owner, tenant or occupier of place where offense was
committed); Edwards v. State, 267 Md. App. 392 (2025) (duty to
retreat except in home, when retreat is unsafe or the escape route
unknown, the defendant was being robbed or was lawfully
arresting the victim); State v. Glowacki, 630 N.W.2d 392,
399 (Minn. 2001) (duty to retreat except in home); State v.
Etienne, 35 A.3d 523,  536–39 (N.H. 2011) (duty to retreat except
in home or curtilage or when assisting law enforcement officer).

12

for the safety of his own life or to protect him from
great bodily harm”).
Lawful self-defense continued to require that the
harm be imminent.  As the Supreme Court of Virginia
explained, “a bare fear that a man intends to commit
a felony, however well grounded, will not warrant the
killing the party by way of prevention. There must be
some overt act indicative of imminent danger at the
time.” Stoneman v. Commonwealth, 66 Va. (25 Gratt.)
887, 895 (1874).
To be lawful, the amount of defensive force still had
to be proportional to the threat. The defendant could
use such force as he “had reasonable grounds to
believe, were necessary.” Beard, 158 U.S. at 564; see
also, e.g., Aldrich v. Wright, 53 N.H. 398, 402 (1873)
(force “should be proportioned to the apparent
danger…. When force, purely defensive at first,
increases and becomes more  than is reasonably
necessary for defence, the excess is aggressive and not
defensive”);  Pond v. People, 8 Mich. 150, 177 (1860)
(“he must not take life if he can otherwise arrest or
repel the assailant”); State v. Thompson, 9 Iowa 188,
192 (1859) (must be apparent  “that the species of
resistance used was necessary to avert” the imminent
danger).
C. The limitations on the right to selfdefense reflect a judgment that it is not
only the defender’s life and liberty that
warrant protection, but those of other
members of society as well.
The limitations on the use of force in lawful selfdefense—necessity, imminence, and proportionality—
reflect the law’s longstanding judgment that human
life and liberty are valuable and deserve legal
protection. Notably, these lim itations protect not just

13

the defender’s life and liberty, but the lives and liberty
of other members of society as well.
 1. American courts have long emphasized that the
doctrine of self-defense is premised on the judgment
that human life is “the most sacred of all interests
committed to its protection.” State v. Benham, 23 Iowa
154, 162 (1867). The “life of a human being must not
be taken upon slight grounds.” Shorter, 2 N.Y. at 201.
That is why the common law held that:
“[T]here can be no successful setting up of
self-defense, unless the necessity for taking
life is actual, present, urgent, unless in a
word, the taking of his adversary’s life is the
only reasonable resort of the party to save his
own life, or his person from dreadful harm, or
severe calamity, felonious in its character.”
Benham, 23 Iowa at 162; see also, e.g., Commonwealth
v. Drum, 58 Pa. 9, 22 (1868) (“When it comes to a
question whether one man shall flee or another shall
live, the law decides that the former shall rather flee
than the latter shall die”).
Recognizing that the law of self-defense must be
protective of human life, the Tennessee Supreme
Court rejected as “monstrous” the argument that
because “the deceased made violent threats against
the life of defendant long before, and up to a short
period of the killing,” the defendant “had a right to kill
the deceased on sight.” Rippy, 39 Tenn. (2 Head) at
218–19. “No Court should for a moment entertain or
countenance” so “bloody a principle.” Id. at 219. Killing
in self-defense is justified only if the threat to the
defendant’s life or great bodily injury is “apparent and
imminent.” Id.
2. Courts also recognized that the limitations on selfdefense protect the rule of law and contribute to a well-

14

ordered society. As the Texas Supreme Court
explained, if the restrictio ns on the use of force are
“relaxed or departed from,” it will “impair the estimate
of the sanctity of human life” and “induce a loose
estimate of its value.” Lander v. State, 12 Tex. 462, 477
(1854). It will also “tend to a state of society in which
licentious, wanton violence, may go unrestrained,
brute force usurp the prerog ative of the law, … [and]
no right of person or property may be esteemed sacred
and inviolable, or will be enjoyed in security.” Id.
3. Decisions like these make clear that the right to
self-defense has never conferred a right for a person to
defend themselves with an unlimited amount of force,
or in any manner that they choose. Rather, as Judge
Wilkinson wrote for the en banc court in
Bianchi, “meaningful limits on the right [to selfdefense] have always existed. Our legal tradition has
never seriously contemplated that a citizen may
employ force against another whenever he chooses
upon mere speculation that such person poses a
prospective threat.” Bianchi v. Brown, 111 F.4th 438,
449 (4th Cir. 2024) (en banc).
The limitations on self-defense demonstrate that
“there are societal interests that can prevail over the
right to protect oneself with force.” Id. The imminence
requirement “ensures that the justice system, not the
individual, is the preferred user of force to restrain
unlawful action when that system has the time and
capacity to act.” Id .; cf. 4 Blackstone, Commentaries,
at  184 (no right to use force unless “certain and
immediate suffering would be the consequence of
waiting for the assistance of the law”). The other
restrictions on “how much force may be employed,  and
against whom force may be us ed, clarify that it is not
just the rights to life and liberty of the defender that
matter, but also those of other members of society.

15

Else, how could we have any society at all?” Bianchi,
111 F.4th at 449.
II. The AR-15 And Similar Assault Weapons
May Be Banned Because Their Features
Were Designed For Military Use And Are Ill-
Suited For Lawful Self-Defense As That
Concept Has Been Understood For
Hundreds Of Years.
The limitations on the lawful use of force in selfdefense, and the values th ose limitations seek to
protect, are critical in determining the scope of the
Second Amendment right. As noted, the Second
Amendment does not  protect the right “to carry arms
for any sort of confrontation.” Heller, 554 U.S. at 595.
Because the right to bear arms for lawful self-defense
is the “central component ” of the Second Amendment
right, id. at 599, the quintessential confrontation for
which a citizen has the right to bear arms is a
confrontation in a home or public place that would
justify a person responding with lawful self-defense.
Such a confrontation would not permit an individual
to possess a weapon for aggression or in a manner that
incites fear or terror or cont ributes to a breach of the
peace. Such firearm possession is unprotected by the
right to lawful self-defense and thus by the Second
Amendment. See supra §§ I.A–I.B; infra § II.D. Indeed,
Heller cited with approval authorities stating that the
Second Amendment right “ought not be abused to the
disturbance of the public peace,” and that the
Constitution confers no right to “keep[] a gun to
destroy [one’s] neighbor.” 554 U.S. at 607, 612 (citation
omitted).
Nor is a domestic confrontation in which a private
person might need a weapon for lawful self-defense
similar to the  confrontation a soldier would face in a

16

wartime battle or military patrol in a hostile foreign
territory. Heller did not question that “weapons that
are most useful in militar y service,” such as “M-16
rifles and the like,” can be banned. Id. at 627.
Application of these princi ples demonstrates that a
ban on assault weapons like  the AR-15 “has little if
any impact on the Second Amendment’s central
objective: protecting the fundamental right to selfdefense.” Wolford, 609 U.S. at 210. The AR-15’s
features were designed for military use and are illsuited for the constitution ally protected purpose of
lawful self-defense. And gi ven their unusual lethality
and frequent use in mass killings, possession of an AR-
15 or similar assault weap on may spread fear and
terror that is incompatible with the right to carry arms
for lawful self-defense.
A. The AR-15’s features were designed for
military use.
1. The AR-15 and similar assault weapons were
designed for soldiers to use in military patrol and
combat. The AR-15 was developed by an engineer at
the Armalite Corporation in response to the Army’s
request for a lightweight, high velocity, small caliber
rifle that could operate in semi- and fully-automatic
modes with firepower capable of penetrating a steel
helmet or body armor at 500 yards.4
The Army tested the AR-15 under combat conditions
in Vietnam. A confidential report issued by the
Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) the
following year concluded that the “lethality of the AR-

3. Moreover, even in semiautomatic mode, an AR-15

4. Significantly, the civilian AR-15 also retains the
lethality of a military-style weapon. As noted, “the AR-
15 and the M16 fire rounds at approximately the same
velocity,” Barnett, 180 F.4th at 1053; see also  supra §

the velocity of a typical handgun.” Rupp, 723 F. Supp.
3d at 853. Furthermore, an AR-15 can fire rounds that

11 or 12.5 times larger than the bullet itself. Bianchi,
111 F.4th at 455; see also  JA104–05. “ So, while a

typical 9mm bullet wound to the liver from a
commonly used handgun like the Glock 19 will produce
a pathway of tissue destruction in the order of one inch
to two inches, an AR-15 wound will literally pulverize
the liver, perhaps best described as dropping a
watermelon onto concrete.” Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 455
(cleaned up); see also Barnett, 180 F.4th at 1053–54.
Thus, as a retired Army Major General explained,
“[f]or all intents and purposes, the AR-15 and rifles
like it are weapons of war”—very deadly weapons
“with the same basic functionality that our troops use
to kill the enemy.” Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rts. v. Lamont,
685 F. Supp. 3d 63, 101 (D. Conn. 2023).
B. The AR-15’s military features make it illsuited for lawful self-defense.
The features that make the AR-15 and similar
civilian assault rifles so well-suited for military use
also make them ill-suited for lawful self-defense.
1. As an initial matter, “civilian self-defense rarely—
if ever—calls for the rapid and uninterrupted
discharge of many shots.” Ocean State Tactical, LLC v.
Rhode Island, 95 F.4th 38, 45 (1st Cir. 2024); see also
Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 459;  Viramontes, Dkt. No. 81-5
at 28. Notably, individuals “engaged in self-defense
fire only 2.2 rounds on average.” Barnett, 180 F.4th at
1051; see also Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rts., 685 F. Supp. 3d
at 96 (report showed “individuals firing 5 shots or
fewer in 97.3% of all incidents nationally”).Thus, an
individual engaged in lawful self-defense does not
need a semiautomatic firearm with the offensive
capability to shoot dozens of bullets in rapid-fire
succession.
Indeed, the use of an AR-15’s rapid-fire capability
could result in the use of force beyond that which
would be considered lawful self-defense. The

22

imminence requirement for lawful use of deadly force
necessitates that the threat is “ongoing, meaning that
an individual engaged in self-defense must alter the
response if the threat dissipates.” Rupp, 723 F. Supp.
3d at 855. But an AR-15’s rapid-fire capability “does
not allow a shooter to reev aluate the circumstances
and determine whether fatal force is still required,”
id., and thus risks discharging force that is
disproportionate to the threat and that continues well
beyond that necessary to avoid death or serious bodily
injury. Supra § I; see also  Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 459
(AR-15s firepower is “disproportionate to fulfilling the
Second Amendment’s purpose of armed self-defense”).
2. The AR-15 has none of the advantages that Heller
identified as establishing the handgun as “the
quintessential self-defense weapon.” 554 U.S. at 629.
“Compared to a handgun, the AR-15 is heavier, longer,
harder to maneuver in tight quarters, less readily
accessible in an emergency, and more difficult to
operate with one hand.” Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 459; see
also Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rts., 685 F. Supp. 3d at 97–98
& n.31.
The AR-15 also features a very long effective range—
“approximately 400–500 yards, compared to 50 yards
for a typical handgun.” JA101. T h a t  i s  u s e f u l  f o r  a
soldier firing on enemy combatants, or a person
desiring to commit a mass mu rder in a public space,
but it is disproportionate for self-defense in a home,
where rooms are measured in feet, not hundreds of
yards.
Even in public places, most confrontations involving
gunfire are at close range, so self-defense would
require a gun with an effective range of approximately
3-10 yards. Viramontes, Dkt. No. 81-11 ¶ 25. And that
is particularly true for confrontations in which the use
of self-defense is lawful, since the imminence

23

requirement would generally require that the threat
be at close range—a situation in which it could be
“difficult to use an assault rifle.” Rupp, 723 F. Supp.
3d at 855.
3. An AR-15 or similar assaul t rifle is also ill-suited
for lawful self-defense because its heightened
firepower “poses a serious risk of ‘over-penetration’—
that is, bullets passing through their intended target
and impacting a point beyond.” Bianchi, 111 F.4th at
458 (cleaned up). Rounds from an AR-15 “have the
ability to easily penetrate most materials used in
standard home construction, car doors, and similar
materials.” Id.; see also Viramontes, Dkt. No. 81-5 at
30–31. Use of an AR-15 for self-defense thus poses an
extreme risk for others in the home, people in a
neighboring apartment, or bystanders on the street
should a person fire multiple rounds and miss the
intended target. See Bianchi , 111 F.4th at 459;
Viramontes, Dkt. No. 81-10 ¶ 15 (declaration of Chief
of the Bureau of Counter Terrorism for the Chicago
Police Department describing “witnessing scenes
where an assault weapon has shot an innocent
bystander through barriers su ch as cars or building
walls”).
AR-15 use similarly poses substantial risk to law
enforcement officers. Ammunition from an AR-15 can
pierce standard bulletproof vests and police protective
equipment. Viramontes, Dkt. No. 81-5 at 31;
Viramontes, Dkt. No. 81-10 ¶¶ 14, 21. Bullet-proof
vests with trauma plates are available, but they are
expensive and limit an officer’s mobility, so it is not
practical for officers to wear them unless they know
assault rifles are present. Viramontes, Dkt. No. 81-10
¶¶ 22–23. And even if an officer dons the extra
protective vest, the coverage  is limited to the chest,
upper back and area over the heart, leaving the officer

24

at risk of death if a stray bullet hits another part of his
body (where, as described above, it will cause massive
physical damage). Id. ¶ 22.
Lawful self-defense has long required that the force
used may not be excessive or disproportionate to the
threat. Supra §§ I.A–I.B. Yet the “net effect of the AR-
15’s military combat features is a capability for
lethality” that “is a far cry from any notion of civilian
self-defense.” Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 456 (cleaned up)
(citation omitted). This “ability to inflict damage on a
scale or in a manner disproportionate to the end of
personal protection” is what separates AR-15s and
similar assault rifles from the handgun and brings
them beyond the protection of the Second Amendment.
Id. at 451.
C. The AR-15 is rarely used in self-defense.
Although Petitioners claim that “tens of millions of
Americans choose” AR-15s and similar semiautomatic
rifles “for lawful purposes like self- and home-defense,”
there is little evidence that such semiautomatic rifles
are commonly used in lawful self-defense. Pet’rs’ Br. at
2 (emphasis added). Instead, the evidence suggests
that “such use is exceedingly rare.” Barnett, 180 F.4th
at 1051; see also, e.g., Worman v. Healey, 922 F.3d 26,
37 (1st Cir. 2019) (record “offers no indication” that
assault weapons like AR-15s “have commonly been
used for home self-defense purposes”). In the summary
judgment briefing below, the Viramontes Petitioners
cited news reports of just  six instances in which a
person used AR-15s in self-defense since 2010 . JA78–
82. Regardless of how “in common use” is defined, that
does not establish that AR-15s and similar automatic
rifles “are weapons ‘in common use’ today for selfdefense.” Bruen, 597 U.S. at 32 (quoting Heller , 554
U.S. at 627).

25

The paucity of evidence that AR-15s are actually
used in self-defense is unsurprising given that AR-15
ownership is itself uncommon. Most Americans do not
own guns, and most Americans who do own guns do
not own assault weapons like AR-15s. Viramontes,
Dkt. No. 81-4 ¶ 21.
Indeed, ownership of AR-15s is concentrated among
a small percentage of gun owners. See Rupp , 723 F.
Supp. 3d at 859; Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rts., 685 F. Supp.
3d at 96 & n.25. The average assault weapons owner
owns three or more of these guns, meaning that there
are far more AR-15s than there are AR-15 owners.
Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rts., 685 F. Supp. 3d at 96; see also
Rupp, 723 F. Supp. 3d at 859 (“undisputed that 66% of
individuals who own an AR- or AK-platform rifle own
two or more such rifles”).
In short, the ban on AR- 15s places no legally
cognizable burden on the right to lawful self-defense.
D. AR-15s may be banned because their
possession or use may spread fear and
terror that is incompatible with the
carry of arms for lawful self-defense.
AR-15s and similar assault rifles may also be
banned because their possess ion or use will in many
circumstances “spread[] ‘fea r’ or ‘terror’ among the
people” due to their “frequent and devastating use in
mass shootings of innocent civilians—an effect that
our common-law tradition has long regarded as
incompatible with lawful carry for self-defense.”
Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 459 (quoting Bruen, 597 U.S. at
50) (cleaned up); see also Friedman v. City of Highland
Park, 784 F.3d 406, 412 (7th Cir. 2015).
The display or use of AR-15s is likely to spread fear
and cause terror because these weapons have been
used in mass shootings that have received widespread

26

media coverage and are commonly seen in movies
depicting military combat or massive shootouts
involving violent groups like drug cartels.
1. The Founders could not have envisioned the terror
and destruction that can be caused by a single gunman
using an assault weapon to commit mass murder in a
matter of seconds. “After all, in the 1770 Boston
Massacre, seven British soldiers firing flintlock
muskets into a crowd managed to take only five lives.”
Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rts. v. Lamont, 153 F.4th 213, 238
(2d Cir. 2025), cert. granted in part sub nom. Grant  v.
Higgins, 146 S. Ct. 2811 (2026). Yet in 2019, a single
gunman “armed with an AR-15 equipped with 100-
round magazines could fire 41 shots in just 32 seconds,
killing nine people and wounding 17 others before he
was stopped.” Id.; see also Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 457
(describing the Pulse shooting where, “[w]ith his rifle
in hand, the ISIS-aligned perpetrator walked into the
Orlando nightclub and fired approximately 200 rounds
in five minutes,” shooting 102 innocent people and
killing 49 of them).
Their utility for mass killing has made the AR-15
and other assault rifles “the preferred weapons” for
those seeking to carry out terror attacks or mass death
and destruction upon innocent civilians. Bianchi, 111
F.4th at 456–57. “AR-15 or AK -47 type assault rifles”
have been used “in every major terrorist attack on U.S.
soil in the past decade.” Id. at 457. Assault weapons
also were used in 53% of ma ss shootings with at least
six fatalities between 2019 and 2022, and 75% of mass
shootings with at least 20 fatalities between 1991 and
2022. Barnett, 180 F.4th at 1058; see also Bianchi, 111
F.4th at 456 (assault rifles used in “every single mass
shooting involving more than 40 deaths”).
2. Mass shootings cause immense harm beyond the
tragic deaths and devastating injuries suffered by the

27

victims. Because mass shootings are seemingly
random and unpredictable, they cause a feeling of
helplessness, which makes them more traumatic than
nearly all other causes of injury and death in the
healthy populations that are exposed. Viramontes,
Dkt. No. 81-16 at 14. Studies have found that
approximately 80% of adults  in the United States
report feeling stressed about mass shootings. Id. at 15.
This results in people avoiding locations like shopping
malls, movie theaters, and large community events for
fear of being shot. Id.
Fear of mass shootings also makes people afraid to
exercise their First Amendment rights. A study
showed that people were much less likely to attend a
protest, carry a sign at a protest, vocalize views at a
protest, or bring children to a protest if they knew
firearms would be present. Viramontes, Dkt. No. 81-18
at 3. This was true in “all regions of the country,”
across “all areas of the political spectrum,” and “for
both gun owners and those who did not own guns.” Id.
Neither gun owners nor non-gun-owners were “‘likely’
or ‘very likely’ to participate in a protest when firearms
were present.” Id. at 10. And AR-15s are a particular
source of fear. Studies show that Americans have
widespread aversion to living next door to a neighbor
who owns an AR-15—indicating that even gun owners
view AR-15s as posing a part icular threat to public
safety in their communities.7
Finally, mass shootings at  schools have caused
immense fear and stress among American youth.

being in self-defence … against one who manifestly intends or endeavors, by violence or surprise, to commit a felony on either. The 13th section declares that ‘a bare fear of any of those offences, to prevent which the homicide is alleged
to have been committed, shall not be sufficient to

2a

justify the killing. It must appear that the circumstances were sufficient to excite the fears of
a reasonable man, and that the party killing, really acted under the influence of those fears and
not in a spirit of revenge’” (quoting Ga. Penal
Code div. 4, § 13).
Connecticut: Morris v. Platt, 32 Conn. 75, 83
(1864)
“A man who is assailed, and under such circumstances as to authorize a reasonable belief that
the assault is with design to take his life, or do
him extreme bodily injury which may result in
death, will be justified in the eye of the criminal
law if he kill his assailant, and in an action of
trespass, if he unsuccessfully attempt to kill him,
and he surviving brings his action, for the killing
would have been lawful and of course the attempt lawful; and no man is liable in a civil suit
or criminal prosecution for an injury lawfully
committed in self-defense upon an actual assailant.”
Massachusetts: Commonwealth v. Selfridge
(Mass. 1806) (Parsons, C.J., charging the grand jury),
in Trial of Thomas O. Selfridge, Counseller at Law,
Before the Hon. Isaac Parker, Esquire, for Killing
Charles Austin, on the Pub lic Exchange, in Boston,
August 4, 1806, at 7 (Boston, 2d ed. 1806)
“A man may repel force by force in defence of his
person, against any one who manifestly intends
or endeavors by violence or surprise, feloniously
to kill him. And he is not obliged to retreat, but
he may pursue his adve rsary until he has secured himself from all danger; and if he kill him
in so doing, it is justifiable self-defence . But a
bare fear, however well grounded, unaccompa-

3a

nied by any open act, indicative of such an intention, will not warrant him in killing. There must
be an actual danger at the time. And, … it must
plainly appear by the circumstances of the case,
as the manner of the assault, the weapon, etc.,
that his life was in i mminent danger; otherwise
the killing of the assailant will not be justifiable
homicide.”
Maryland: Research found no criminal cases before 1900 involving a plea of self-defense
South Carolina:  State  v. Wood, 1 S.C.L. (1 Bay)
345, 346–47 (1794)
“The general rule of law ‘that wherever the assault or battery proceeds from the plaintiff or
prosecutor’s own fault; as where he gives the
first blow &c. there it is sufficient justification to
the defendant.’ But there must be however, in all
cases, some proportion between the battery given, and the first assault. For Lord Holt lays it
down as a rule, that the meaning of the plea son
assault is, that the defendant struck in his own
defence Esp. 389. So that the degree of resistance, ought to be in proportion to the nature
of the injury offered; that is, that it be sufficient
to ward off such injury, and no more. For the
moment a man disarms or puts it out of the power of the aggressor from doing him further injury, he ought to desist from using further violence; and if he does commit any further outrage,
he, in his turn, then becomes the aggressor. In
Salk. 642, a question was, what assault was sufficient to maintain such plea? Lord Holt said,
that Wyndham, J. would not allow such plea, if it
was an unequal return . His lordship then says,
that for every assault, he did not think it reasonable that a man should be banged with a cudgel .

4a

That a small blow will not justify an enormous
beating, &c. That the meaning of the plea was,
that the defendant struck in his own defence. And
of the same opinion were all the Judges on this
occasion, and verdict was against the defendant
accordingly.”
New Hampshire: State v. Elliot, 11 N.H. 540, 544
(1841)
“The defence of one’s self … is, under certain circumstances, a natural right; but one general
principle holds in these cases, that the selfdefence must be regulated by the nature, degree,
and design of the attack, and the repelling force
must go no farther than is necessary to prevent
the mischief intended by the aggressor.
The same general rule applies to the wresting of
property from another by force. In such case, the
owner of the property ha s a right to defend it,
but he can in no case go beyond what the urgency of the occasion requires.”
Virginia: Vaiden v.  Commonwealth , 53 Va. (12
Gratt.) 717, 729–30 (1855)
“When a man is assaulted in the course of a sudden brawl or quarrel, he may in some cases protect himself by slaying the person who assaults
him, and excuse himself on the ground of selfdefense. Before a party thus assaulted, however,
can kill his adversary, he must have retreated as
far as he safely could to avoid the assault, until
his further going back was prevented by some
impediment, or as far as the fierceness of the assault permitted. He must show to the jury that
the defense was necessary to protect his own life,
or to protect himself against grievous bodily
harm.… And with regard to the necessity that

5a

will justify the slaying of another in self-defence,
it should seem that th e party should not have
wrongfully occasioned the necessity; for a man
shall not in any case justify the killing of another
by a pretense of necessity, unless he were without fault in bringing that necessity upon himself.”
New York:  Shorter v. People, 2 N.Y. 193, 203
(1849)
“When a man is struck with the naked hand, and
has no reason to apprehend a design to do him
any great bodily harm, he must not return the
blow with a dangerous weapon. After a conflict
has commenced he must quit it, if he can do so in
safety, before he kills his adversary: and I hardly
need add, that if his adversary try to escape, he
must not pursue, and give him fatal blows with a
deadly weapon.”
North Carolina: State v. Hill, 20 N.C. (3 & 4 Dev.
& Bat.) 491, 494–95 (1839)
“It is laid down as settled law, that if a man assault another with malice prepense, even though
he should be driven to  the wall, and kill him
there to save his own life, he is yet guilty of murder in respect of his first intent.”
“Even if the prisoner had not begun the affray,
but had been assaulted in the first instance, and
then a combat had ensued, he could not excuse
himself as for a killing in self-defence, unless he
had quitted the combat before a mortal blow was
given, if the fierceness of his adversarypermitted, and retreated as far as he might with
safety, and had then killed his adversary of necessity, to save his own life.”

6a

Rhode Island: State v. Sherman, 16 R.I. 631, 632
(1889)
“Where there is no homicide, the rule generally
laid down is that the assaulted person may defend himself, opposing force to force,––using so
much force as is necessary for his protection,––
and can be held to answer only for exceeding
such degree. … ‘The assailed person is not permitted to stand and kill his adversary, if there is
a way of escape open to him, while yet he may
repel force by force, and, within limits differing
with the facts of the case, give back blow for
blow’” (citation omitted).
Vermont: Mellen v. Thompson , 32 Vt. 407, 408
(1859)
“The amount and kind of force which the law authorizes one to use in de fence of his own person,
depends entirely upon the extent and character
of the attack upon him, and all the attending circumstances. He may use such kind and amount
as is necessary for his ow n protection and safety,
even to destroying the life of his assailant. If it
were necessary for a defendant pleading such defence to set forth all the particulars of the plaintiff’s prior assault, and all the various circumstances under which it was made, and which
might in evidence affect his right to repel it, and
to what extent, it would become next to impossible to frame such a plea, and ordinarily it would
by no means enable the court to determine upon
the face of the pleadings, whether or not, the
force used by the defendant was justified by the
first assault made by the plaintiff.”
Kentucky: Rapp v. Commonwealth, 53 Ky. (14 B.
Mon.) 494, 501 (1854)

7a

If the defendant “did believe, and that he had
reasonable ground to believe, that [the victim]
intended to proceed immediately to the infliction
of bodily harm upon him with the knife in his
hand, and that he would do so unless prevented
by such act of self-defense as was then in the
power of [defendant], then the shooting by [defendant] was excusable on the ground of selfdefense and apparent necessity. But if he had
not reasonable ground to apprehend immediate
violence to his person by [the victim] by the use
of the knife, then his act of shooting and thus
aiming at the life of [the victim], was not only not
excusable as being in self-defense, but it was not
done under such provocation as on the ground of
heat and passion would make it a misdemeanor
instead of a felony.”
Tennessee: Rippy v. State, 39 Tenn. (2 Head) 217,
219–20 (1858)
“The law on this subject is, that, to excuse a homicide, the danger of life, or great bodily injury,
must either be real, or honestly believed to be so
at the time, and upon sufficient grounds. It must
be apparent and imminent…. To constitute the
defence, the belief or apprehension of danger
must be founded on sufficient circumstances to
authorize the opinion that the deadly purpose
then exists, and the fear that it will at that time
be executed…. So a case must not only be made
out to authorize the fear of death or great harm,
but such fear must be really entertained, and the
act done under an honest and well founded belief
that it is absolutely necessary to kill at that moment, to save himself from a like injury.”
Ohio: Erwin v. State, 29 Ohio St. 186, 199 (1876)

8a

“It is true that all authorities agree that the taking of life in defense of one's person can not be either justified or excused, except on the ground of
necessity; and that such necessity must be imminent at the time; and they also agree that no
man can avail himself of such necessity if he
brings it upon himself.  [A] true man, who is
without fault, is not obliged to fly from an assailant, who, by violence or surprise, maliciously
seeks to take his life or do him enormous bodily
harm.”
Louisiana: State v. Chandler, 5 La. Ann. 489, 490–
91 (1850)
“A man may repel force by force in defence of his
person, habitation or property, against one who
manifestly intends or endeavors by violence or
surprise to commit a known felony, such as murder, rape, robbery, arson and the like, upon either. In these cases he is  not obliged to retreat
but may pursue his adversary until he has secured himself from all danger, and, if he kill him
in so doing, it is called justifiable self-defence.”
“[T]here must be actual danger at the time from
the violence and a reasonable belief that a felony
is intended.”
“[I]f [the victim] actually  attacked [defendant],
and was beating his head against a brick wall so
as to put his life really  in danger, and [defendant] then killed his assailant from absolute necessity to preserve his own life, the charge asked
for was not only the law of self-defence, but was
applicable to the case, an d should have been given to the jury by the court. But if [the victim]
was unarmed and sick, and only in consequence
of a quarrel with [defendant’s] wife the preceding

9a

evening, the latter was so enraged that he
rushed upon and gave him four stabs with a
Bowie knife, until then concealed in his bosom–
[the victim] being a perfectly passive victim–the
charge asked was entirely inapplicable, and
should have been refused by the judge on account of its irrelevancy to the case.”
Indiana: Hayden v. State, 4 Blackf. 546, 547 (Ind.
1838) (per curiam)
“The law is well settled, that a person thus assaulted may use as much force as is necessary for
his defense, but he may not kill, wound or maim
his antagonist, unless it be  necessary to save his
life, or protect himself from great bodily harm.
Every assault will not justify every battery. Son
assault is a good plea in mayhem, but it must
appear that the degree of resistance was in proportion to the nature of the injury offered.”
Mississippi: Cotton v. State , 31 Miss. (2 George)
504, 510–11 (1856)
“The party interposing the plea of self-defence,
on a trial for murder, must be understood as undertaking to show, that in the perpetration of the
deed he acted under a nece ssity, either actual or
apparent, forced upon him by the party killed;
for if such were not the case, his defence can
avail him nothing, or certainly not further than
to mitigate the crime. The very defence itself
presupposes danger to th e party's life or person,
except in cases where he may act in defence of
the life or person of another…. The law says that
there must be reasonable ground to apprehend a
design to commit a felony, or do some great personal injury, and imminent  danger of such design being accomplished.… Reasonable ground to

10a

apprehend the design, and imminent danger of
its accomplishment, must both exist at the same
time.”
Illinois: Campbell v. People, 16 Ill. 17, 19 (1854)
“If the defendant was pursued or assaulted by
the deceased in such a way as to induce in him a
reasonable and … well-grounded belief that he
was actually in danger of losing his life, or suffering great bodily harm, when acting under the influence of such reasonable apprehension, he was
justified in defending himself ….”
Alabama: Oliver v. State, 17 Ala. 587, 598 (1850)
“To justify the taking of life there must be an
imperious necessity to prevent the commission of
a felony or great bodily harm. Without this necessity, the law, although under some circumstances it will mitigate the crime to manslaughter, cannot hold the party slaying altogether justified.”
Maine: State v. Field, 14 Me. 244, 247 (1837)
“A man may oppose force to force in defence of
his person, his family, or property, against one,
who manifestly endeavors by surpri[s]e or violence to commit a felony, as murder, robbery or
the like. But to justify killing the aggressor his
apparent intent must be to commit a felony….
and it must appear that the danger was imminent, and the species of resistance used, necessary to avert it.”
Missouri: State v. Shoultz , 25 Mo. 128, 152–53
(1857)
Approving jury instruction stating: “The law of
self-defense is emphatically the law of necessity,

11a

to which a party may have recourse under certain circumstances to prevent any reasonably
apprehended great personal injury which he may
have reasonable grounds to believe is about to
fall upon him. If you be lieve that defendant had
reasonable cause to apprehend a design on the
part of deceased to commit a felony upon defendant, or to do him some great personal injury, and
that there was reasonable cause to apprehend
immediate danger of such design being carried
out, and he shot and killed deceased to prevent
the accomplishment of such apprehended design,
then the killing is justified upon the ground of
self-defense, and you should acquit.”
Arkansas: Stanton v. State , 13 Ark. 317, 323
(1853) (quoting trial court jury charge)
 “That in ordinary cases of one person killing another, in self-defence, it  must appear that the
danger was so urgent and pressing that in order
to save his own life, or to prevent his receiving
great bodily injury, the killing of the other was
necessary; and it must appear also that the person killed was the assailant, or that the slayer
had really, and in good faith endeavored to decline any further contest, before the mortal blow
or injury was given.”
Michigan: Pond v. People, 8 Mich. 150, 177 (1860)
“A man is not, however, obliged to retreat if assaulted in his dwelling, but may use such means
as are absolutely necessary to repel the assailant
from his house, or to prevent his forcible entry,
even to the taking of life. But here, as in the other cases, he must not take life if he can otherwise
arrest or repel the assailant ….”
Florida: Pinder v. State, 27 Fla. 370, 384 (1891)

12a

“[T]he killing would to be excusable” self-defense,
the defendant must show “that he was surrounded by such a condition of affairs as made it, from
his stand-point, reasonable for a cautious and
prudent man to believe it was necessary to …
strike the fatal blow in order to save himself
from death or great bodily harm.”
Texas: Lander v. State , 12 Tex. 462, 476, 478
(1854)
“The right of self-defense rests upon the law of
necessity.” “To justify a homicide on the ground
of self-defense, it must clearly appear that it was
a necessary act, in order to avoid death or some
severe calamity” (citation omitted).
Iowa: State v. Thompson , 9 Iowa 188, 192–93
(1859) (citing Wharton, American Criminal Law
436)“To make a homicide excusable, on the
ground of self defense, the danger must be shown
to be actual and urgent. No contingent necessity
will avail. It must be proved that the assault was
eminently perilous; and without there be a plain
manifestation of a feloni ous intent, no assault
will justify killing the assailant.”
“If, under the circumstances, there was no reason for the belief by defendant, that his person
was in danger of death or great bodily harm, but
that an ordinary battery was all that was intended, and all that he had any reason to fear
from the acts of the deceased, he had no right to
take the life of his assailant.”
Wisconsin: Wis. Rev. Stat. ch. 133, § 5 (1849)
Homicide is justifiable “[w]hen committed in the
lawful defence of such person … when there shall
be a reasonable ground to apprehend a design to

13a

commit a felony, or to do some great personal injury, and there shall be imminent damage of
such design being accomplished ….”
California: People v. Hurley, 8 Cal. 390, 391 (1857)
“A reasonable fear and actual belief, will excuse
the party” in certain cases. “But a reasonable
fear and actual belief of great bodily harm, are
not sufficient in all cases. The statute says the
killing must be ‘absolutely necessary’ to prevent
it. The infliction of ‘great bodily harm’ upon another, may, or may not, amount to a felony. So an
attempt to inflict it, may, or may not, be a felony.
If attempted with a deadly weapon, or with the
intent to commit a felony, then the reasonable
fear, and actual belief, would justify the killing.
(Sec. 50.) But when the a ttempt to inflict ‘great
bodily harm’ does not constitute felony, there
must exist the absolute necessity mentioned by
the thirty-first section, to excuse the killing.”
Minnesota: State v. Shippey, 10 Minn. 223, 231–32
(1865)
“Self-defense ex vi termini  is a defensive not an
offensive act, and must not exceed the bounds of
mere defense and prevention. To justify such act
there must be at least an apparent necessity to
ward off by force some bodily harm.”
“Where the party has not retreated from or attempted to shun the combat, but has as in this
case unnecessarily entered into it, his act is not
one of self-defense.”
Oregon: Goodall v. State, 1 Or. 333, 337–38 (1861)
(quoting Shorter v. People, 2 N.Y. 193, 197–98 (1849))
Self-defense available “when, from the nature of
the attack, there is reasonable ground to believe

14a

that there is a design to destroy his life, or commit any felony upon his person, the killing the
assailant will be excusable homicide, although it
should afterwards appear that no felony was intended.”
Kansas: State v. Howard, 14 Kan. 173, 174–75
(1875)
Self-defense available where there is “a reasonable apprehension of imminent danger.”
West Virginia:  State v. Cain, 20 W. Va. 679, 704
(1882)
Approving of jury instru ction: “When one without fault himself is attacked by another in such a
manner or under such circumstances as to furnish reasonable ground for apprehending a design to take away his life, or do him some great
bodily harm, and there is reasonable ground for
believing the danger imminent that such design
will be accomplished, and the person assaulted
has reasonable grounds to believe and does believe, such danger is imminent, he may act upon
such appearances and may without retreating
kill the assailant, if he has reasonable grounds to
believe and does believe, that such killing Is necessary to avoid the apprehended danger …”
Nevada: State v. Ferguson, 9 Nev. 106, 117 (1874)
If the defendant “was without fault, and had reasonable ground to believe, and did believe, that
he was in danger of his lif e, or of receiving great
bodily harm, from [the victim], and that this
could only be prevented by his using such means
of defense as were within his power, and he acted
under such belief and not in a spirit of revenge,
then the killing of [the victim] was justifiable.”

15a

Nebraska: Williams v. State, 6 Neb. 334, 336, 339
(1877)
Approving jury instruction permitting acquittal
for self-defense if “the accused was in imminent
or apparent danger of receiving great bodily
harm from the deceased at the time of the homicide, or that the deceased was about to commit a
felonious assault upon the defendant, was in the
situation, had the implements and weapons, and
possessed the animus, ability, and was in a position to do so at the time of the killing, or that the
deceased was about to take the life of the prisoner, and there was no other way for him to save it
than to commit the homicide; or that he had a
just and well grounded apprehension that deceased was about to kill him or to do him great
bodily harm, and that there was no other way to
save himself from the impending danger of life,
limb, or great bodily injury than to commit the
homicide …”
